name: Yusuf Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Yusuf. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't linked to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you tell me is confidential and won't carry your name. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Right now a normal day is two hundred kilometres from home. I lead a transmission crew, so the big steel towers, the high-voltage lines that carry power across the country, and we're building a new line out to a wind farm. We're up at five in a motel, on site by six thirty, and I'm planning the lifts, checking harnesses and talking to the crane operator. I love it when a span of conductor goes up clean and sags just right between two towers. What wears me out is being away: three weeks on, one week home.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How does your family manage with that?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Grace is a nurse on nights, so it's a juggle. Her mum comes over a lot, and my daughter Chioma, she's fourteen, has started cooking for her little brother Daniel. I call them every night from the motel car park, because the signal inside is useless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I already say in the canteen: they're building more power lines than ever because the data centres need the electricity. If AI is mostly hype, we still built the lines for it. I'd probably post something cheeky in the union group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means steady work for me until I retire, I think. Maybe a bit less overtime once the data centre rush calms down. I'd actually like that, because it means more nights at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am. I'd keep putting about three hundred a month aside, and I'd try to move to a crew with fewer weeks away now that Chioma's getting older. I'd keep using the AI chatbot now and then, for writing up incident reports.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pretty good, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use a chatbot for incident reports. How did that start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marek, my groundman, showed me. He's been with me fifteen years and he's always the one who tries things first. I write it rough, the chatbot tidies it, and I check every word because if it's wrong it's my name on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would fewer weeks away mean at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could see Daniel's football on Saturdays. Last season I made two matches out of twenty. He doesn't complain, which is almost worse.

S0.say: I'd say they're building more lines than ever because data centres need power, so even if AI is hype we still built the lines. I'd post something cheeky in the union chat.
S0.think: I think it means steady work until I retire, with maybe less overtime once the data centre rush calms. I'd welcome that because it means more nights at home.
S0.do: Carries on as normal and keeps saving about three hundred a month. Tries to move to a crew with fewer weeks away, and keeps using a chatbot now and then for incident reports.
S0.quote: If AI is mostly hype, we still built the lines for it.
S0.fieldNote: Yusuf sees the AI boom mostly as a source of work, because data centres need new lines. His real pain point is time away from his family, not job security. He uses AI the way he picks up most tools, after a trusted colleague shows him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the union needs to get ahead of this and make sure the new jobs go to the people who already do the work. Stringing robots, drones, all of it, train us to run it. That's what I'd say at the branch meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For transmission I think it's mostly good news for a while. Drones already pull the first rope across a span, and that used to be a long, dangerous job. If machines take the worst bits, I might keep my body going till I'm sixty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put my name down for any drone or robot course the company runs, once I'd seen one of the other crews try it. I'd use the chatbot a bit more for planning lifts. And I'd ask the union rep to push for a fair share of the savings going into wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit curious. Maybe a little worried for the younger lads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the younger ones?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the jobs that shrink are the starter jobs, the ground work, the hauling. That's how I learned. If a machine does it, how does a nineteen-year-old get to where I am?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait for another crew to try the course first. Why not go first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm not the guinea pig type. I've seen new kit come in that nearly hurt someone. Let somebody else find the problems, then I'll learn it properly.

S1.say: I'd say the union must get ahead of this and make sure new jobs go to the people already doing the work. Train us to run the stringing robots and drones.
S1.think: I think it's mostly good news for transmission for a while, because machines take the dangerous parts. It might let my body last until I'm sixty.
S1.do: Signs up for drone and robot courses once another crew has tried them. Uses the chatbot more for lift planning and asks the union rep to push for a share of the savings in wages.
S1.feel: Calm and curious, with some worry for younger workers.
S1.quote: If a machine does it, how does a nineteen-year-old get to where I am?
S1.fieldNote: He sees steady change as safety progress for his own body. His concern shifts to the apprenticeship ladder, which is a thoughtful and quite selfless worry. He's open to training but wants someone else to test it first, which fits his steady nature.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this can't be left to the companies. Government needs to guarantee incomes while it sorts out what work even means now. I'd say it loudly, at work and online, and I'd march if the union called it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the big transmission builds would still need people for a year or two, but after that I don't know. Grace's job feels safer than mine, which is strange to say. We've got about four months saved, so if I lost my job we'd be living on her pay, and it doesn't cover the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd stop all the extras and push the savings as high as we could before anything happens. I'd take every away job going, even though I hate them, because they pay the most. And I'd talk to Grace about whether Chioma should still plan on university or something faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. That's the honest word.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Grace say to each other the night it sinks in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Grace would say we've had worse, because we have, when Daniel was in hospital. I'd say we haven't, not like this, because then I knew the job was still there. Then we'd make a list, that's what we do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What goes on that list first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The mortgage, then the car loan, then the kids. We'd ask the bank about payment holidays before we needed them. I'd ring Marek too, because he'd be in the same boat and two heads are better.

S2.say: I'd say this can't be left to the companies and government must guarantee incomes. I'd say it at work and online, and march if the union called it.
S2.think: I think transmission work lasts a year or two at most, then I don't know. With four months saved we'd be on Grace's pay, which doesn't cover the mortgage.
S2.do: Cuts all extras and builds savings fast while taking every high-paying away job. Asks the bank about payment holidays early and rethinks whether his daughter goes to university.
S2.feel: Frightened, more than when his son was in hospital, because the job won't be there.
S2.quote: Grace's job feels safer than mine, which is strange to say.
S2.fieldNote: The two-year picture turns his household upside down: his partner's job suddenly looks safer than his. He goes straight to practical planning with Grace, list first, which seems to be how they cope. He calls for government income support, consistent with his views.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough warning that nobody should be left behind. The union should be bargaining now for retraining and a share of what the robots save. I'd say vote for whoever puts that in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me time to move sideways. I'm thinking about safety inspection, or being the person who certifies the robots are working right, because somebody has to sign them off. It's not the same as climbing, but it's still the lines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd ask the company about the inspection track and start the course, at night if I have to. I'd keep saving the three hundred and add whatever overtime I can. And I'd stay active in the union, maybe stand for branch committee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but there's a plan, so it's manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Can you picture the day you stop climbing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can, and it's harder than I thought just now. My dad drove a bus for thirty years and he cried on his last day. I'd probably be the same, standing at the bottom of a tower watching a machine go up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who else at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marek, because he hates classrooms more than I do. I'd try to get him on the course with me. If we did it together he'd stick with it.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough warning that nobody should be left behind. The union should bargain now for retraining and a share of the savings, and I'd vote for whoever promises that.
S3.think: I think five years lets me move sideways into safety inspection or certifying the robots. It's not climbing, but it's still the lines.
S3.do: Asks about the inspection track and starts the course in the first year, at night if needed. Keeps saving and stands for the union branch committee.
S3.feel: Anxious but manageable because he has a plan, with sadness about stopping climbing.
S3.quote: I'd probably be the same, standing at the bottom of a tower watching a machine go up.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, Yusuf builds a realistic sideways move into inspection and certification. The story of his father's last day as a bus driver brought out real grief under the plan. He'd bring his colleague Marek along, a sign of how much he values his crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years means we can plan this like adults. Shorter weeks, earlier pensions for the people who've broken their bodies doing this, and training for everyone. I'd say it at the branch and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a lot of runway for me. By then I'd be fifty-three, both kids through school, and I'd have had time to move into inspection or training. I'd still worry for the country, though, more than for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the inspection course over a couple of years instead of cramming it. I'd move to a local crew so I'm home every night. And I'd keep the savings going, with a target of six months by the time the kids leave school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in the background. Not like the fast one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd worry for the country more than for yourself. What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I mean the people who don't have a union or a trade. My cousin drives deliveries and he'd have nothing. If the money from all this goes to a few people, ten years just means a slower crash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the extra time change anything for your kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Chioma wants to be an engineer. With ten years I'd tell her go ahead, but learn how these machines are built and who owns them. Daniel's ten, so I've no idea, he still wants to be a footballer.

S4.say: I'd say ten years means we can plan like adults: shorter weeks, earlier pensions for people with worn-out bodies, and training for everyone.
S4.think: I think ten years is plenty of runway for me, with the kids through school and time to move into inspection. I'd worry more for the country than for myself.
S4.do: Does the inspection course over two years instead of cramming it and moves to a local crew to be home every night. Builds savings towards six months by the time the children leave school.
S4.feel: Uneasy in the background, nothing like the fast scenario.
S4.quote: If the money from all this goes to a few people, ten years just means a slower crash.
S4.fieldNote: The ten-year runway lets him see himself landing safely, so his concern turns outward to people without a union or a trade. Here he worries less about himself than about almost anyone else. His advice to his daughter is to understand who owns the machines, which fits his politics.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. What would help is the company paying for the inspection and certification training now, before anything happens, and a guaranteed income while people retrain. Some help with mortgages during the gap would stop families like mine going under.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the bodies. Half the men my age have bad knees and bad shoulders from this job. If robots take the climbing, some of us would be glad, as long as there's still a paycheque at the end of the week.

headlineQuote: If robots take the climbing, some of us would be glad, as long as there's still a paycheque at the end of the week.
portrait: Yusuf Okafor is a 43-year-old transmission crew lead who builds high-voltage tower lines and spends three weeks of every four away from home. He sees the current AI boom as good for his trade, and steady change as a chance for machines to take the dangerous work. The two-year AGI picture frightens him, because his partner's nursing pay can't cover the mortgage on its own. Given five or ten years, he plans a sideways move into safety inspection and certifying the robots, bringing his long-time groundman with him. His deeper worry, with time to prepare, is for people with no union and no trade.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because he'd lose his job within a couple of years and his partner's pay wouldn't cover the mortgage.
whatWouldHelp: Company-paid inspection and certification training now, a guaranteed income while people retrain, and help with mortgages during the gap.
